validated_work_order.confidence_rationale: Every number in this order was produced by running the shipped `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` against fixtures under the real test clock (`currentDay()` is pinned to 2017-01-01 by `global.IS_TESTING`, packages/loot-core/src/shared/months.ts:173-179), and the proposed matcher was run as a prototype over the same fixtures. The only judgement left is whether the forecast file should change in this ticket, which is listed under risks for a human to strike.
validated_work_order.understanding:
The Upcoming rows the register shows for a schedule are built by `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` (packages/loot-core/src/shared/schedules.ts:517). It collects the schedule's occurrence dates inside the upcoming window, applies `dates.shift()` when the schedule's status is `paid`, and then filters the survivors with `isScheduleOccurrencePosted` (schedules.ts:145), called once per occurrence over the WHOLE list of schedule-linked transactions. For the schedule kind a person creates by hand — `posts_transaction: false` and an `isapprox` date condition (schedule-edit-utils.ts:49, ScheduleEditModal.tsx:76) — `getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate` returns `occurrenceDate - 2 days`, so an unstamped transaction discharges any occurrence in `[occurrenceDate - 2, occurrenceDate]`. That window is an INTERVAL, so when occurrences are less than three days apart it covers several at once and one transaction is counted against two or three of them. `link-schedule` never writes `schedule_occurrence` (server/rules/action.ts:235), so every rule-matched transaction on a synced budget is unstamped and takes that arm. `RecurringSchedulePicker.tsx:40` offers a daily interval, so the overlapping case is reachable from the UI.

I measured this rather than inferring it. Under the test clock, occurrences for a daily manual schedule in the default 7-day window are 2017-01-02 through 2017-01-08 and `next_date` is 2017-01-02. One unstamped schedule-linked transaction dated 2017-01-06 removes FOUR of those seven rows today — 01-02, 01-06, 01-07 and 01-08 — when only 01-06 was paid. Dated on `next_date` it removes three (01-02, 01-03, 01-04). Two payments remove six. Every-other-day behaves the same way at half the density: one payment dated 2017-01-06 removes three of four rows. The same predicate is called the same way in packages/loot-core/src/server/forecast/forecast-schedules.ts:205-215, where the same over-removal silently drops days from the projected balance.
validated_work_order.root_cause: The occurrence matcher is a per-occurrence PREDICATE applied to an unbounded transaction list, so nothing stops one transaction from being counted for several occurrences. The overlap only bites when the gap between two occurrences is smaller than the 2-day lookback, which is why every shipped test missed it: `makeSchedule()` in schedules.test.ts uses `posts_transaction: true` and an `op: 'is'` date condition, and both of those make `getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate` return the exact occurrence date, collapsing the window to a single day. `createForecastWithPostedDailySchedule` in forecast/app.test.ts has the same shape. The fallback arm was never exercised through `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` at all.
validated_work_order.approach:
Make the match ONE-TO-ONE. Add `matchPostedScheduleOccurrences` to packages/loot-core/src/shared/schedules.ts: given a schedule, its id, the occurrence dates under consideration, the schedule's posted transactions and optionally the date the coarse status bit already accounted for, it returns the `Set<string>` of occurrence dates that are discharged, guaranteeing each transaction discharges at most one occurrence. `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` calls it in place of the `unpaidDates` filter, and `buildFutureScheduleOccurrences` calls it in place of its per-occurrence `isScheduleOccurrencePosted` call.

`dates.shift()` stays exactly where it is. It is not redundant with the matcher: `getHasTransactionsQuery`'s fallback arm is a LOWER BOUND only (`schedule_occurrence == null AND date >= getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate(schedule, next_date)`), so it reports `paid` for a transaction dated after the occurrence, which the matcher's two-sided comparison deliberately does not. That is also the source of the row counts below: a payment dated on a LATER occurrence removes TWO rows — the head, consumed by the coarse status bit before the matcher ever runs, plus the occurrence the payment was actually dated on.

The head-spend is NARROWED to the head's own two-sided window. A transaction is spent on the coarse claim only when it is stamped for `paidByStatusDate`, or unstamped with `tx.date` between `getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate(schedule, paidByStatusDate)` and `paidByStatusDate` inclusive. A payment made for a LATER occurrence falls outside that window, is not spent, and goes on to discharge the occurrence it was actually made for.

Measured against the shipped code on the fixtures below (currentDay = 2017-01-01; `D` is the schedule's `next_date`):

Daily manual, 7-day window, occurrences D..D+6 (2017-01-02..2017-01-08):
- one payment dated D (2017-01-02), status `due`: 3 rows go today, 1 after.
- one payment dated D (2017-01-02), status `paid`: 3 today, 1 after.
- one payment dated a later occurrence (2017-01-06), status `due`: 3 today, 1 after.
- one payment dated a later occurrence (2017-01-06), status `paid`: 4 today, 2 after.
- two payments dated 2017-01-04 and 2017-01-06, status `paid`: 6 today, 3 after.

Every-other-day, occurrences D, D+2, D+4, D+6: 2 rows go today for a payment on `next_date` (1 after); 3 today for a payment on a later occurrence (2 after); 4 today for two payments (2 after).

Weekly manual, 30-day window, occurrences 2017-01-02/-09/-16/-23/-30 — the shipped unit-test fixture — is UNCHANGED by this fix, and the counts there are already the two-row rule:
- unstamped payment dated 2017-01-07 (the Saturday before the second Monday), status `paid`: today and after both keep [2017-01-16, 2017-01-23, 2017-01-30]. Two rows go — 01-02 by the Paid badge, 01-09 by the payment.
- payment dated 2017-01-09 (on the Monday), status `paid`: same three survivors, same two rows.
- payment dated 2017-01-06 (three days early), status `paid`: [2017-01-09, -16, -23, -30]. ONE row goes, the head; the Monday it was early for is still listed, which is the early-payment boundary holding.
- stamped payment for 2017-01-09: [2017-01-02, -16, -23, -30], unchanged.

Forecast, daily manual, occurrences 2024-03-10/-11/-12, one unstamped transaction dated 2024-03-10: today's forecast keeps NONE of the three; after the change it keeps 03-11 and 03-12, which is the correction.

INVARIANT asserted by a sweep in tests[]: for every occurrence date and both status values, the number of removed occurrences never exceeds the number of posted transactions carried for that schedule plus the one head `dates.shift()` removes, and no occurrence is removed unless a distinct transaction can be named for it.

files.change:
Add ONE new exported function immediately after `isScheduleOccurrencePosted` (which ends at line 172), and no other new export:

export function matchPostedScheduleOccurrences({ schedule, scheduleId, occurrenceDates, postedTransactions, paidByStatusDate }: { schedule: ScheduleEntity; scheduleId: string; occurrenceDates: readonly string[]; postedTransactions: readonly PostedScheduleTransaction[]; paidByStatusDate?: string; }): Set<string>

Use the existing `getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate`, `ScheduleEntity` and `PostedScheduleTransaction` types; add no imports. Body, in this order:
1. `const ordered = [...occurrenceDates].sort();` — `yyyy-MM-dd` sorts lexicographically into chronological order. Do not mutate the caller's array.
2. `const paid = new Set<string>();`
3. Build `claimable`: `postedTransactions.map((tx, index) => ({ tx, index }))`, filtered to `entry.tx.schedule === scheduleId`, sorted by `tx.date` ascending and, for equal dates, by `index` ascending. `Array.prototype.sort` is stable but the input from `getPostedScheduleTransactionsQuery` has no ORDER BY, so keep the explicit tie-break. Any removal below splices `claimable`; never mutate `postedTransactions`.
4. `paidByStatusDate` spend — the head occurrence's TWO-SIDED window, which is what lets a payment made for a LATER occurrence reach that occurrence instead:
   `if (paidByStatusDate != null) {`
   `  const headStart = getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate(schedule, paidByStatusDate);`
   `  const spentAt = claimable.findIndex(({ tx }) =>`
   `    (tx.schedule_occurrence != null && tx.schedule_occurrence === paidByStatusDate) ||`
   `    (tx.schedule_occurrence == null && tx.date >= headStart && tx.date <= paidByStatusDate),`
   `  );`
   `  if (spentAt !== -1) { claimable.splice(spentAt, 1); }`
   `}`
   The upper bound `tx.date <= paidByStatusDate` is load-bearing, not optional. Remove the spent entry from `claimable` and do nothing else with it. Do NOT add `paidByStatusDate` to `paid` — the caller's `dates.shift()` already removed that row. If nothing qualifies, remove nothing: that is the case where the posted-transaction list has not loaded yet and the shift must still fire on its own.
5. Stamped pass: for each `occurrenceDate` of `ordered`, if any remaining `claimable` entry has `tx.schedule_occurrence != null && tx.schedule_occurrence === occurrenceDate`, `paid.add(occurrenceDate)`. Two stamps naming one occurrence still mark it once; a stamp naming a date outside `occurrenceDates` matches nothing.
6. Unstamped pass: for each remaining `claimable` entry with `tx.schedule_occurrence == null`, in sorted order, find the FIRST `occurrenceDate` of `ordered` that is not already in `paid` and satisfies `tx.date >= getScheduleOccurrenceMatchStartDate(schedule, occurrenceDate) && tx.date <= occurrenceDate`; if one is found, `paid.add(occurrenceDate)`. Each entry is visited once so it can claim at most one occurrence, and the `!paid.has(...)` guard stops it claiming one another entry already took. This runs after step 4, so a transaction the head spent is already out of `claimable` and cannot also be handed to a later occurrence.
7. Return `paid`.

In `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions`, replace the `unpaidDates` filter at lines 594-604 with:

  const paidDates = matchPostedScheduleOccurrences({
    schedule,
    scheduleId: schedule.id,
    occurrenceDates: dates,
    postedTransactions: postedTransactionsBySchedule.get(schedule.id) ?? [],
    paidByStatusDate: status === 'paid' ? schedule.next_date : undefined,
  });
  const unpaidDates = dates.filter(date => !paidDates.has(date));

Leave the `if (status === 'paid') { dates.shift(); }` block at lines 580-582 exactly as it is, and leave the comment above it at 584-593 in place — it is the reasoning that keeps the two filters non-redundant and a future narrowing must not undo it. Leave `isScheduleOccurrencePosted` exported and unchanged.

The forecast repeats the identical predicate call over the identical kind of list, so it carries the identical defect: a manual daily schedule with one early payment silently drops the following two occurrences from the projected balance. Fixing only the register would leave a money number wrong.

acceptance.check: On a schedule with occurrences one day or two days apart that a person created by hand, one schedule-linked transaction removes only the row it can be named for, and every other row for that schedule stays listed. The count is exact and depends on where the payment lands, so both cases are specified. Let D be the schedule's next due date, which the fixture sets to TODAY, so the seven rows for a daily schedule are D, D+1, D+2, D+3, D+4, D+5 and D+6, and the four rows for an every-other-day schedule are D, D+2, D+4 and D+6. A payment dated ON D removes EXACTLY ONE row, D itself, and the other six (or three) stay listed. A payment dated on a LATER occurrence — say D+3 for the daily schedule — removes EXACTLY TWO rows, D and D+3, because the schedule's own Paid status consumes the head before the matcher runs, and the other five stay listed. Today the same two payments remove three and four rows respectively.
acceptance.how_to_verify: Use 'View demo' on the setup screen so there is a budget to register against. Schedules -> Add schedule: frequency 'Days', interval 1, a payee used by nothing else, a distinctive amount, 'Post transactions automatically' OFF, starting TODAY. Leave 'Upcoming length' at its default. Open the register and count EVERY row carrying that payee — seven — not only the ones badged 'upcoming': the row dated today is badged 'due' and the other six are badged 'upcoming'. Record each row's date. Then add ONE transaction with that payee and amount dated TODAY; the rule links it to the schedule. Count again: the difference must be EXACTLY 1 and the row that went must be today's. Today the difference is 3. Delete that transaction, then add ONE dated D+3 instead: the difference must be EXACTLY 2 and the rows that went must be exactly today's and D+3's. Today the difference is 4. Add a SECOND payment dated D+5: the count drops by exactly 1 more and the row that goes is D+5's. Never 3 rows for one payment. Then repeat the whole count with frequency 'Every 2 days': the differences are 1 then 2, against 2 then 3 today. To confirm each transaction really was linked to the schedule, open the Schedules page and check that this schedule's status badge reads 'paid' after the payment — that badge is driven by the same linked-transaction query the rows are filtered against, so a transaction the rule failed to link would leave the badge unchanged and every count above would be unproven.

acceptance.check: An unstamped transaction dated up to two days before an occurrence still discharges that occurrence, so the early-payment fallback keeps working. On a weekly manual schedule with 'Upcoming length' set to '2 weeks' so that at least two Mondays are listed, a transaction dated the SATURDAY BEFORE THE SECOND LISTED MONDAY removes TWO rows — the schedule's own next due date D, consumed by the schedule's Paid status, and that Monday, which is the occurrence the payment was dated for. Every OTHER Monday that was listed before the payment is still listed afterwards. A transaction dated THREE days before that Monday removes ONE row only, D, and that Monday is still listed. This is identical before and after the change: it is a regression guard on the lookback, not a behaviour change.
acceptance.how_to_verify: Schedules -> Add schedule: a payee used by nothing else, a distinctive amount, frequency 'Weeks', interval 1, 'Post transactions automatically' OFF, starting on the coming Monday — or today, if today is a Monday. In the same edit form set 'Upcoming length' to '2 weeks' and save; without this the 7-day default leaves at most one Monday listed and there is nothing to count. Open the register and record EVERY row carrying that payee and its date: the head D, the Monday D+7, and D+14 as well if today is that Monday. Add ONE transaction with that payee and amount dated the SATURDAY BEFORE D+7, that is two days early and one week past D; the rule links it, unstamped. Count again: the rows that must be gone are exactly D and D+7, and every other row recorded before the payment is still listed. On the Schedules page the status badge must read 'paid'. Then delete that transaction, add one dated THREE days before D+7 instead, and confirm that exactly one row has gone — D — while D+7 is still listed. If the count of rows changes by anything other than 2 and then 1, the fallback has moved.

acceptance.check: A schedule whose date condition is an exact 'is' match, or which posts transactions automatically, behaves as it does now: an unstamped transaction discharges only the occurrence whose date it carries, and one dated a day earlier discharges none. qa_script: Use 'View demo' on the setup screen so there is a real budget to register against, then Schedules -> Add schedule: frequency 'Days', interval 1, a payee used by nothing else, a distinctive amount, 'Post transactions automatically' OFF, starting TODAY, 'Upcoming length' left at its default.

Open the register and count EVERY row carrying that payee — seven. Do not count only the ones badged 'upcoming': the row dated today is badged 'due'. Record each row's date relative to today, calling today D.

Add ONE transaction with that payee and amount dated TODAY. Count again. The difference must be EXACTLY 1 and the row that went must be D. Today it is 3. Check the Schedules page and confirm this schedule's badge reads 'paid' — that is the evidence the rule linked the transaction.
Delete that transaction, then add ONE dated D+3 instead. Count again. The difference must be EXACTLY 2 and the rows that went must be exactly D and D+3. Today it is 4.
Add a SECOND payment dated D+5. The count drops by exactly 1 more and the third row to go is D+5. Never 3 rows for one payment.
Repeat steps 2-5 with frequency 'Every 2 days'. The rows are D, D+2, D+4 and D+6; the differences are 1 then 2, against 2 then 3 today.

Weekly schedule, 'Post transactions automatically' OFF, 'Upcoming length' set to '2 weeks': record every row carrying the payee (D, D+7, and D+14 as well if today is that Monday). Pay the SATURDAY BEFORE D+7 and confirm EXACTLY TWO rows go — D and D+7 — and every other row recorded before the payment is still listed. Today and after the fix are the same here; this step guards the two-day lookback. Then delete it and pay THREE days before D+7 instead, and confirm exactly ONE row goes, D, with D+7 still listed.

Weekly schedule with 'Post transactions automatically' ON and 'Upcoming length' set to '2 weeks': pay the DAY BEFORE D+7, confirm the transaction is genuinely linked (the schedule's badge on the Schedules page reads 'paid'), and confirm no occurrence row moves except the head D. Then pay ON D+7 and confirm exactly two rows go, D and D+7.

Regression sweep: a weekly auto-post schedule with two payments for two different occurrences still removes exactly those two rows; a non-recurring schedule's single row still disappears when it is paid; re-dating a posted transaction off its occurrence date does NOT bring the row back.

Open Reports -> Forecast for an account holding the daily manual schedule and confirm the projected balance now carries an entry on the day after the paid occurrence and on the day after that. Before the fix those two days are missing from the projection.
risks: This narrows what counts as paid, on the path that decides which rows a user can still pay, and the dangerous direction is over-narrowing: a user who is behind and pays an occurrence dated after `next_date` could see that occurrence offered again. AC-1, AC-2 and AC-5 each specify the resulting count exactly — two rows for a payment on a later occurrence, never more — rather than leaving it to judgement, and the head spend is narrowed to the head's own two-sided window precisely so that such a payment reaches the occurrence it was made for instead of being consumed by the head.

packages/loot-core/src/server/forecast/forecast-schedules.ts changes too, and no acceptance criterion in the issue's own list covers the forecast — AC-6 does, but IAC-1 to IAC-4 do not mention it. It changes projected balances for budgets holding an unstamped schedule-linked transaction on a schedule with occurrences less than three days apart: the forecast now includes occurrences it was silently dropping. That is a correction, but it is a visible change to a money number and a judgement the ticket did not ask for, so it is listed here for a human to strike before implementation.

The two-row rule is surprising enough that a reviewer or a user may read the fix as a regression. It is not new behaviour: it is what the shipped code already does on a weekly schedule, where occurrences are seven days apart and the 2-day window cannot overlap. The fix makes the dense-schedule case behave the way the sparse one already does. `getHasTransactionsQuery` is untouched, so the head is still consumed by the coarse status bit exactly as before.

`isScheduleOccurrencePosted` is left exported with no production caller afterwards. `knip` is not run in CI, so this will not fail a build; it is called out so a reviewer does not read it as an oversight.
The change is confined to packages/loot-core/src/, adds no dependency, contacts no host, and touches nothing under forbidden_paths.
residual_risks: The schedule edit form's 'Upcoming length' field is what makes AC-2 and AC-5 observable in a 7-day-default register; if that control is renamed or moved in the UI before QA runs, those two steps need re-pathing. The field is `custom_upcoming_length`, persisted through ScheduleEditModal.tsx:130 and honoured at schedules.ts:536.

The browser fixture for AC-1 starts the schedule TODAY, so the head row is badged 'due' rather than 'upcoming'. Counting only 'upcoming'-badged rows will undercount by one and look like a failure. The qa_script says so at step 2.
out_of_scope: Backfilling `schedule_occurrence` on transactions created by `link-schedule`. The narrowing in this plan is what makes the unstamped path correct without it, and a data migration is its own ticket.

`getHasTransactionsQuery`'s lower-bound-only fallback arm. It is deliberately wider than the matcher's two-sided comparison and the shift depends on it; changing it would move `next_date` for existing budgets, because `hasTransactionForSchedule` and `advanceSchedulesService` both read it.

Deleting `isScheduleOccurrencePosted` once it has no production caller. It is left in place here as the readable statement of the per-occurrence rule the matcher generalises; removing it is a cleanup touching only this file.

The refresh tear the issue mentions — `useSchedules` publishing statuses and posted transactions independently, so rows can disappear for a round trip. Tracked in #41, independent of this fix, and listed in risks because QA will see its symptom here.

Advancing `next_date` past an occurrence the user has already paid. `advanceSchedulesService` owns that and reads `getHasTransactionsQuery`; it is a separate behaviour change on a different code path.

alternatives_considered.approach: Leave `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` alone and fix the defect only in `getHasTransactionsQuery`, tightening its fallback arm so it cannot report `paid` for a transaction dated after the occurrence.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: That query is load-bearing for `hasTransactionForSchedule` and `advanceSchedulesService`, which read it to decide which occurrence a posted transaction marks paid and therefore where `next_date` moves. Narrowing it would change `next_date` for every existing budget that has an early or late payment, which is a far larger behaviour change than this ticket asks for. It also would not fix the defect on its own: the over-removal happens in the `unpaidDates` filter, not in the status query.

alternatives_considered.approach: Cap the lookback instead of making the match one-to-one — keep the per-occurrence predicate but shrink the window until it cannot overlap, e.g. match only transactions dated exactly on the occurrence for dense schedules.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It silently breaks the early-payment fallback the issue's IAC-2 requires: a schedule paid two days early would have its occurrence offered again, which is the double-payment risk the issue names as the dangerous direction. It also cannot express the required rule, which is 'one transaction, one occurrence', only 'a narrower window'.

alternatives_considered.approach: Give every schedule-linked transaction a `schedule_occurrence` stamp at creation time in `link-schedule`, so the date fallback is never needed.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It fixes future transactions only. Every transaction already in a user's budget is unstamped and keeps taking the fallback arm, so the reported bug would persist for exactly the budgets most likely to hit it, at an intensity proportional to how long they have been running. It is a data migration and belongs in its own ticket.

alternatives_considered.approach: Group occurrences into non-overlapping buckets before matching — e.g. assign each transaction to the nearest occurrence rather than the first that fits.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: Nearest-occurrence is wrong for a payment made well before its occurrence, which is the case the 2-day lookback exists to serve, and it makes the assignment order-dependent in a way that is hard to state as an invariant. First-unclaimed-in-window order is deterministic, and the invariant it supports — no occurrence is removed unless a distinct transaction names it — is directly assertable in a sweep.

assumptions: The register renders every preview row it is given, including the head whose `forceUpcoming` is false: `previewStatus` falls back to the schedule's own status for the badge (TransactionsTable.tsx:1355, 1795-1820) and rows are merged into the list at components/accounts/Account.tsx:176. The reviewer's evidence said the head does not render; that is true of the `forceUpcoming` flag but not of the row, which is why AC-1 counts all seven rows and names the head's 'due' badge rather than counting only 'upcoming' ones.

`monthUtils.currentDay()` is pinned to 2017-01-01 whenever `global.IS_TESTING` is set (shared/months.ts:173-179), so the unit fixtures are written against 2017 dates and no clock mocking is needed or wanted.

A schedule's 'Upcoming length' is settable per schedule from the schedule edit form and is honoured by `computeSchedulePreviewTransactions` via `schedule.custom_upcoming_length ?? upcomingLength` (schedules.ts:536), which is what lets a browser fixture widen the window deterministically.
unknowns: Whether the forecast file belongs in this ticket at all. The issue's IAC list is entirely about Upcoming rows; I have included the forecast because it carries the identical defect and a wrong projected balance is worse than a wrong row count, but it is a scope call a human should make rather than a planner's.

Whether any other caller of `isScheduleOccurrencePosted` exists outside the two files named here. I read the two call sites in this repository; a caller in a downstream integration would not be visible from here and would silently keep the old behaviour.
